title: ADA Title II digital-accessibility compliance programs for small Illinois local governments
product_service: Fixed-price WCAG 2.1 AA programs for municipalities, townships, park/library/fire/sanitary districts: site + document inventory, automated+manual audit, CMS fixes, PDF remediation (or archive strategy), accessibility policy/statement, staff training, quarterly monitoring retainer.
target_customer: Village/city administrators, clerks, IT/communications staff and district directors at Illinois units of local government with <50,000 population (deadline Apr 26, 2028) and 50k+ (Apr 26, 2027); Illinois has 6,930 local governments incl. 3,218 special districts [A, WS15-S003].
purchase_motivation: Federal ADA Title II rule compliance dates (Apr 26, 2027 / Apr 26, 2028) [A, WS15-S001]; litigation/complaint exposure; small entities lack in-house staff.
spending_evidence: DOJ estimates the one-year delay alone saves entities ~$395M/yr annualized (~$210M/yr to small entities), implying multi-billion compliance spending nationally [A, WS15-S001]. Illinois-specific spend: MISSING.
representative_operators: Level Access, Deque, TPGi (enterprise accessibility vendors; revenue not verified) [E]
AudioEye/UserWay overlay vendors (overlays widely criticized as insufficient) [E]
revenue_mechanism: One-time program fee ($3k-$25k by entity size) plus monitoring/remediation retainer ($150-$1,000/mo) [E].
typical_transaction_value: $5k-$15k initial for a small village/district; $2k-$10k/yr retainer [E]
direct_costs: Auditor/remediator labor (US or offshore), testing tools licenses, PDF remediation labor, assistive-tech manual testing time.
contribution_profit_note: ~$3k-$8k contribution per small-entity program plus ~$1.5k-$6k/yr retainer contribution [E].
working_capital_note: Local governments pay net-30 to net-60 after board approval; deposits uncommon; low inventory.
sales_cycle: 1-6 months (board/council meeting cycles; small purchases under local bid thresholds can be approved by administrators) [E]
repeat_purchase: recurring-contract: monitoring retainer; content keeps changing so remediation never ends
acquisition_channels: Direct outreach to clerks/administrators using Census/IEPA/association lists
Illinois Municipal League, IAPD (park districts), library system conferences
Partnerships with municipal website vendors and IT MSPs
Free automated scan reports as door-opener
customer_accessibility: Good: all entities and their websites are public; small entities are reachable by email/phone; procurement is often informal below bid thresholds [E].
supplier_accessibility: Confirmed: testing tools (axe, WAVE, screen readers) are freely/commercially available; remediation labor hireable [E].
competitive_intensity: moderate-high: national vendors and CMS providers target governments; overlays sold cheaply; few Illinois-focused small-entity specialists observed [E].
entry_strategy: Productized fixed-fee packages for the long tail of special districts/townships that national vendors ignore; publish Illinois deadline guidance; bundle PDF archive strategy to reduce scope; offer certification-free but documented conformance reports.
licenses: None required; standard business registration and E&O insurance advisable [E]. No professional license applies to accessibility auditing.
regulatory_barriers: Demand depends on a rule DOJ says it may substantively revise [A, WS15-S001]; SBA Advocacy recommended withdrawal for small governments [C, WS15-S002].
operational_risks: Scope creep in legacy PDFs; quality failures if over-reliant on automated scans; government website platform lock-in.
financial_risks: Demand cliff if DOJ narrows/withdraws the rule for small entities; slow municipal payments.
geographic_constraints: Remote-deliverable; Illinois focus is a sales choice, nationally applicable.
founder_expertise: WCAG 2.1/2.2 techniques, assistive-tech testing, PDF/UA remediation; CPACC/WAS credentials optional.
staffing: Founder sells + audits first; hire 1-3 remediation specialists (or offshore partner) by month 6-12.
automation_potential: AI-assisted triage of scan results, alt-text drafting, PDF tagging suggestions, report generation; manual AT testing and judgment stay human.
delegation_potential: Good with SOPs: auditing and remediation are teachable roles; sales relationships transferable.
scalability: Can expand to other states' local governments and to K-12/universities; capped by regulatory demand durability.
expansion: Document remediation production (WS15-002), vendor ACRs (WS15-003), Title III private clients, website rebuilds.
roic_note: Asset-light: <$15k at risk; ROIC potentially >300% if demand materializes [E].
critical_assumptions: Small entities will buy before the 2028 date despite possible DOJ revision
Price points of $5k-$15k are acceptable to small districts
Manual audit + remediation can be delivered at 45%+ margin
unanswered_questions: What share of Illinois small entities have already contracted for compliance?
Will DOJ's announced NPRM narrow scope (e.g., K-12, small entities)?
Typical Illinois local bid thresholds for professional services
Actual price points paid by comparable municipalities (procurement awards)
failure_modes: Race to the bottom with overlays/cheap scans
Long municipal sales cycles drain founder time
score_rationale: feasibility 9: no license. ai 7: real productivity gains in remediation. resilience 4: demand rests on a rule already delayed and under reconsideration. fcf 4: small-entity tickets are low; ceiling likely ~$250k/yr.
preliminary_verdict: advance - best-fit regulation-driven B2G service for a tech founder, but must be validated against DOJ's pending substantive revision before committing.

title: Document/PDF accessibility remediation production service (per-page) for public entities and universities
product_service: Production remediation of PDFs, Word, PowerPoint and forms to WCAG 2.1 AA / PDF-UA with tagging, reading order, alt text, tables; turnaround SLAs; bulk backlog projects and ongoing per-page subscriptions.
target_customer: Public universities, community colleges, counties, state agencies, school districts and their vendors nationally; also law/finance firms under Title III risk.
purchase_motivation: Title II web rule covers conventional electronic documents posted after compliance date [A, WS15-S001]; backlog of agendas, reports and course materials.
spending_evidence: DOJ economic analysis implies large compliance spend nationally [A, WS15-S001]; per-page market prices not verified this session (MISSING).
representative_operators: Large remediation vendors and offshore document shops (names/revenues not verified) [E]
revenue_mechanism: Per-page pricing ($3-$15/page by complexity) or monthly page-volume subscriptions [E].
direct_costs: Trained remediator labor (onshore/offshore), Acrobat/CommonLook-type tooling, QA testing.
working_capital_note: Net-30/60 institutional payments; labor paid weekly - modest receivables gap.
sales_cycle: 2-12 weeks for small purchases; RFP for large contracts
repeat_purchase: recurring: continuous document flow (meeting packets, syllabi, reports)
acquisition_channels: Subcontracting to WS15-001-type audit firms and CMS vendors
Direct to university accessibility/disability resource offices
customer_accessibility: Moderate: buyers identifiable; universities have accessibility offices; institutional procurement adds friction.
supplier_accessibility: Confirmed: remediation tools available; labor trainable in weeks [E].
competitive_intensity: high: established vendors, offshore shops, and AI tools improving fast.
entry_strategy: Speed and price on mid-size backlogs, quality guarantee, white-label capacity for audit firms ahead of 2027/2028 surge.
regulatory_barriers: Same DOJ revision risk as WS15-001 [A, WS15-S001].
operational_risks: Quality defects; surge-and-trough demand; staff turnover.
financial_risks: Price compression as AI auto-tagging improves; post-deadline demand drop.
founder_expertise: PDF/UA, tagging tools, QA processes, production management.
staffing: Hire/train remediators from month 2-4; offshore partner possible.
automation_potential: AI auto-tagging and alt-text drafts cut labor 30-60% [E]; complex tables/forms still need human QA.
scalability: Scales with labor; national market; but commoditizing.
expansion: Accessible authoring templates, training, Title III corporate clients.
roic_note: Very low capital; ROIC high if utilization maintained [E].
critical_assumptions: AI tooling lowers cost faster for us than price falls
Institutions outsource rather than build in-house
unanswered_questions: Actual per-page market rates (procurement awards)
Volume of public-entity documents needing remediation vs. being archived/removed
score_rationale: delegation 7: production SOPs. entry 4: crowded, AI tools commoditize. resilience 4: rule-dependent surge.
preliminary_verdict: hold - viable as the production arm of WS15-001, weak as a standalone due to commoditization.

title: Accessibility Conformance Reports (VPAT/ACR) and remediation advisory for vendors selling to public entities
subindustry: Accessibility conformance documentation for software vendors
product_service: Third-party evaluation of SaaS/edtech/govtech products against WCAG 2.1 AA and Section 508; VPAT 2.x ACR authoring; remediation roadmap; annual re-evaluation.
target_customer: Product/compliance leads at small-mid govtech, edtech, payment, permitting and agenda-management software vendors selling to state/local governments and universities.
purchase_motivation: Public buyers covered by Title II must ensure third-party content/apps conform; procurement increasingly asks for ACRs [E].
spending_evidence: MISSING - no verified pricing or volume data this session.
representative_operators: Level Access, TPGi, Deque, independent consultants (not verified) [E]
revenue_mechanism: Per-product evaluation fee plus annual update.
working_capital_note: 50% deposits feasible with private-sector vendors; low working capital.
acquisition_channels: Govtech vendor lists from procurement portals
customer_accessibility: Moderate: vendors identifiable from public contracts; need credibility.
entry_strategy: Fast, fixed-price ACRs for small vendors facing a specific RFP deadline.
regulatory_barriers: Demand tied to Title II timeline [A, WS15-S001].
founder_expertise: Deep WCAG expertise and credibility (IAAP credentials help).
staffing: Founder-delivered initially; hire senior testers later.
automation_potential: Automated scans + AI report drafting; expert judgment remains human.
scalability: National; ceiling limited by expert labor.
expansion: Remediation dev services, accessibility training for dev teams.
critical_assumptions: Public buyers actually demand ACRs from vendors at scale
unanswered_questions: How many Illinois RFPs require ACRs?
Market price of ACRs
score_rationale: access 4: credibility wall for an unknown expert. delegation 4: scarce expert labor.
preliminary_verdict: hold - useful adjunct to WS15-001; too expertise-bound as a standalone.

title: Section 504 (HHS) web accessibility compliance for healthcare providers receiving HHS funds
product_service: WCAG 2.1 AA audits, patient-portal/forms remediation and monitoring for clinics, FQHCs, home-health and behavioral-health agencies receiving HHS financial assistance (e.g., Medicaid).
target_customer: Practice administrators/compliance officers at small-mid Illinois healthcare organizations.
purchase_motivation: HHS 2024 Section 504 rule set web accessibility dates (reported May 2026 for 15+ employees, May 2027 for <15) - CURRENT STATUS NOT VERIFIED (HHS site returned 403).
representative_operators: Healthcare website vendors and accessibility firms (not verified) [E]
working_capital_note: Private practices pay faster than governments; deposits possible.
customer_accessibility: Moderate: providers identifiable; awareness of 504 web obligations reportedly low [E].
entry_strategy: Cross-sell Title II playbook to a segment with different deadlines; target FQHCs/behavioral health with Medicaid exposure.
licenses: None; HIPAA BAA may be required if accessing PHI systems [E].
regulatory_barriers: Rule status after 2025-2026 litigation/administration changes unverified.
operational_risks: Patient-portal platforms controlled by EHR vendors limit remediation.
financial_risks: Enforcement uncertainty depresses willingness to pay.
critical_assumptions: HHS 504 web requirements remain in force with near-term dates
unanswered_questions: Current status of HHS Section 504 web/mobile compliance dates (May 2026/May 2027) after 2025-2026 actions
Enforcement posture of HHS OCR
score_rationale: resilience 3: status unverified and enforcement uncertain. Kept as a distinct segment of the accessibility play.
preliminary_verdict: hold - verify rule status before any work; potential add-on segment to WS15-001.

title: Lead service line inventory verification & LCRI compliance data services for small Illinois water systems
subindustry: Water utility compliance data & field verification
product_service: Resolve 'unknown' service-line materials: records digitization, statistical/predictive prioritization, curb-stop/meter-pit and in-home visual verification, coordination of vacuum potholing (subcontracted), inventory updates to IEPA/LCRI formats, replacement-plan data packages and public-facing inventory maps.
target_customer: Public works directors/water superintendents and consulting engineers of Illinois community water systems (1,758 CWS) - especially small/mid systems without GIS staff.
purchase_motivation: Illinois LSLRNA (PA 102-0613) inventory and replacement obligations [A, WS15-S009] plus federal LCRI 10-year replacement mandate [A, WS15-S007]; unknown lines must be resolved to plan replacement and avoid treating all unknowns as lead.
spending_evidence: 2020 Illinois inventory: 667,275 lead and 819,586 unknown-material lines out of 3,852,509 [A, WS15-S009]; EPA projects ~4.0M LSLs nationally [A, WS15-S035]; DWSRF lead funding $2.6B referenced by EPA [A, WS15-S007]. Per-line verification prices: MISSING.
representative_operators: Regional consulting engineers (e.g., Baxter & Woodman, Strand, HR Green - roles not verified) [E]
revenue_mechanism: Per-system project fees and per-line verification fees; annual inventory maintenance subscription.
typical_transaction_value: $10k-$80k per small/mid system project; $40-$300 per line verified; potholing pass-through $400-$1,000/hole [E]
direct_costs: Field technicians, vehicles, potholing subcontractors, GIS/software, insurance.
contribution_profit_note: ~$15-$100 contribution per verified line excluding pass-through [E].
working_capital_note: Municipal net-30 to net-60; often SRF-funded with reimbursement lag; must float field labor 1-3 months.
sales_cycle: 2-9 months (council approval; engineering firm subcontracts can be faster)
repeat_purchase: recurring-contract: inventory updates continue through multi-decade replacement programs
acquisition_channels: Subcontracting to consulting engineers already holding utility contracts
IEPA CWS lists and published inventories to target high-unknown systems
customer_accessibility: Moderate: all CWS public; small systems reachable; trust and references matter; engineers act as gatekeepers.
supplier_accessibility: Assumed: vacuum-excavation contractors available regionally; JULIE locates required before digging [E].
competitive_intensity: moderate: engineering firms do this as part of larger scopes; software firms sell tools, not field labor.
entry_strategy: Be the low-cost field+data crew for overloaded engineering firms; fixed per-line pricing; predictive targeting to minimize digs.
licenses: No professional license for records/visual verification [E]; excavation work in ROW needs municipal permits/insurance; anything construed as engineering design must be under a PE [E]. Replacement itself is licensed plumbing work (see WS15-007).
regulatory_barriers: LCRI compliance date and Illinois 17.12 replacement schedule details not re-verified this session; LCRI page shows no revision announcement as of Dec 29, 2025 [A, WS15-S007].
operational_risks: Homeowner access for in-home checks; data quality; field safety.
financial_risks: Slow municipal payment; federal rule changes could relax urgency.
geographic_constraints: Field work regional (Illinois/upper Midwest); data services national.
founder_expertise: Water utility regulation, GIS, field-verification methods, municipal sales.
staffing: 2-4 field techs after first contract; GIS analyst.
automation_potential: Predictive models on parcel age/records, AI extraction from tap cards, automated IEPA template generation; field verification remains human.
scalability: Regional crews replicable; Midwest has dense LSL counts.
roic_note: Moderate capital (vehicles, insurance, working capital); ROIC ~100-300% if utilization good [E].
critical_assumptions: Many Illinois systems still carry large unknown counts in 2026-2027
Engineering firms will subcontract field verification
unanswered_questions: Latest (2024/2025) Illinois statewide unknown counts
LCRI compliance date and any 2025-2026 revisions
Local procurement rules: is inventory work 'professional engineering' under QBS?
Market per-line verification pricing
failure_modes: Undercut by engineering firms bundling the work
Cash squeeze from municipal payment lag
score_rationale: resilience 7: statutory multi-decade program with A-level demand data. cash 4: municipal lag. entry 5: wedge as subcontract crew.
preliminary_verdict: advance - large, mandated, Illinois-specific demand with a feasible non-licensed entry point; validate subcontract appetite with engineering firms (via public data only).

title: Lead service line replacement customer engagement: outreach, right-of-entry consents and filter logistics
product_service: Door-to-door and multilingual outreach to secure signed property-owner consents for private-side replacement, scheduling, notification letters, filter/cartridge distribution tracking and CRM reporting for utilities.
target_customer: Water utilities and their program managers/engineers running LSL replacement programs in Illinois.
purchase_motivation: Replacement cannot proceed without owner access; LSLRNA and LCRI require notifications and replacement pace [A, WS15-S009; A, WS15-S007].
spending_evidence: Scale of lines to replace (667,275 lead in 2020) [A, WS15-S009]; outreach spend per line MISSING.
representative_operators: Program-management engineering firms and community-based outreach nonprofits (not verified) [E]
revenue_mechanism: Per-consent or per-household fee plus program management retainer.
direct_costs: Canvasser wages, translation, CRM software, mailing.
working_capital_note: Payroll weekly vs municipal net-45; needs ~2 months working capital.
supplier_accessibility: Labor market for canvassers confirmed generally [E].
competitive_intensity: moderate: PR firms, nonprofits, engineering firms.
entry_strategy: Measured consent-conversion rates and bilingual crews; pay-for-performance pricing.
licenses: None beyond local solicitation rules (often exempt for utility programs) [E].
regulatory_barriers: Some cities prefer community-based organizations; local hiring requirements.
founder_expertise: Field operations management, CRM, community engagement.
staffing: Canvassers and a field supervisor from first contract.
automation_potential: Routing, e-signature consents, multilingual messaging drafts; human doorstep work remains.
roic_note: Low capital; ROIC moderate due to thin margins [E].
critical_assumptions: Utilities outsource outreach rather than use staff/CBOs
unanswered_questions: Do Illinois programs pay per consent?
Consent conversion benchmarks
score_rationale: fcf 3: thin labor margin. resilience 7: multi-decade mandate.
preliminary_verdict: hold - better as a bundled module of WS15-005 than standalone.

title: Lead service line replacement contracting (with licensed plumbers) for Illinois utilities and homeowners
product_service: Excavation/trenchless replacement of public- and private-side lead service lines under utility programs or homeowner-paid private-side replacements.
target_customer: Illinois municipalities/utilities (bid work) and homeowners (private side).
purchase_motivation: LSLRNA replacement mandate and LCRI 10-year replacement [A, WS15-S009; A, WS15-S007].
spending_evidence: 667,275 lead lines (2020) in Illinois [A, WS15-S009]; per-line cost MISSING (commonly cited $8k-$25k, unverified) [E].
direct_costs: Licensed plumbers/laborers (prevailing wage), equipment (vac/excavators), materials, restoration, bonding.
working_capital_note: Retainage, monthly pay applications, prevailing-wage payroll weekly - heavy working capital.
customer_accessibility: Low for a newcomer: bonding capacity and track record required.
supplier_accessibility: Assumed: materials available; licensed plumbers scarce [E].
competitive_intensity: moderate-high: union contractors in Chicago region.
entry_strategy: Private-side homeowner replacements in towns without utility-funded programs, partnering with a licensed plumber.
licenses: Illinois plumbing license (IDPH) required for water service work - founder would need licensed employee/partner [E]; bonds; prevailing wage on public work.
regulatory_barriers: Licensing, bonding, prevailing wage, municipal permits.
financial_risks: Bonding requires personal indemnity/credit; retainage; cost overruns.
staffing: Licensed plumber(s), crew, equipment operator before first job.
critical_assumptions: Founder can secure bonding and a licensed plumber partner
unanswered_questions: Who exactly may perform service-line replacement under Illinois law (plumbing license vs utility exemption)?
Typical Illinois unit prices from bid tabs
score_rationale: resilience 8: multi-decade mandate. feasibility 4: license partner + bonding. roic 3: capital heavy, back-loaded.
preliminary_verdict: reject (for this founder from zero) - the money is real but gated by licensing, bonding and capital; revisit later as acquisition/holding-co play.

title: Drinking-water compliance sampling route service for small water systems (lead/copper, LCRI schools/childcare, PFAS initial monitoring)
product_service: Scheduled sample collection, chain-of-custody, lab shipping and reporting for small community/non-transient water systems; coordination of LCRI school/childcare lead sampling and PFAS initial monitoring.
target_customer: Operators of small CWS, mobile-home parks, subdivisions, schools/daycares on own wells (NTNC systems) in Illinois.
purchase_motivation: PFAS NPDWR initial monitoring due by 2027 (PFOA/PFOS retained) [A, WS15-S006]; LCRI sampling obligations [A, WS15-S007].
spending_evidence: MISSING - unclear how much sampling small Illinois systems outsource vs IEPA/own operators.
representative_operators: Accredited environmental labs offering field sampling (not verified) [E]
revenue_mechanism: Per-sample collection fee + lab markup; annual compliance calendar subscription.
typical_transaction_value: $75-$200 per sample event + lab pass-through; $1k-$5k/yr per small system [E]
direct_costs: Technician time, mileage, coolers/shipping, lab fees (pass-through).
working_capital_note: Lab fees fronted; small systems pay net-30.
customer_accessibility: Moderate: systems are public; many tiny operators.
supplier_accessibility: Assumed: accredited labs accept outside samplers [E].
entry_strategy: Route density in a few counties; compliance calendar software.
licenses: Some samples may require certified operator collection - MISSING; lab must be IEPA-accredited (we would not run a lab).
regulatory_barriers: PFAS rule partially rescinded/proposed changes [A, WS15-S006].
founder_expertise: Sampling protocols, chain of custody, IEPA rules; possibly water operator certification.
critical_assumptions: Small systems will outsource sampling rather than DIY
unanswered_questions: Which Illinois samples must be collected by certified operators?
Does IEPA collect samples for small systems?
score_rationale: fcf 2: low-ticket route with unclear outsourcing demand. resilience 7: mandated monitoring.
preliminary_verdict: reject - mandated but low-value and possibly served free by labs/IEPA.
